title: One training row: likely to sell out
front: In 90 seconds, typed: you must predict whether a hotel will sell out within 7 days of a search. Write ONE training row: the unit, the time anchor, the label, and three features.
back: Unit: hotel x check-in date x as-of (search) date. Label: 1 if it sold out within 7 days after the as-of date. Features use only data known at the as-of date: rooms left, booking pace over the last 7 days, price vs area median, days to check-in, local events. Split by time, not at random.

title: Structure in 90 seconds: is the ad spend incremental?
front: In 90 seconds, typed: a CFO asks whether search-ad spend is incremental. Give two clarifying questions and three ways to answer, then pick one.
back: Clarify: brand or generic search, and what decision depends on it. Ways: (1) a geo experiment that cuts spend in random regions, (2) past variation with difference-in-differences, (3) a marketing mix model. Pick the geo test: unit, metric (incremental profit per euro), duration in full weeks, one risk.

title: Structure in 90 seconds: a metric dropped 5%
front: In 90 seconds, typed: bookings fell 5% week on week. Write your first four checks, in order.
back: 1. Is it real: tracking, logging or a dashboard change. 2. Is it seasonal: same week last year, holidays. 3. Where: slice by country, device, channel, new vs returning, and check whether one slice explains it (and whether the mix shifted). 4. What changed: releases, experiments, pricing, competitors, outages.

title: One training row: fraud alert model
front: In 90 seconds, typed: build a model to prioritise transaction-monitoring alerts. Write ONE training row and say how you would split the data.
back: Unit: one alert (customer x alert date). Label: 1 if the investigation ended in a suspicious-activity report. Features known at alert time: amount vs the customer's history and peer group, country risk, counterparties, account age. Split by time, with no customer in both train and test.

title: Answer the question asked: value of each touchpoint
front: In 90 seconds, typed: a user clicks a search ad, then a comparison site, then a metasearch link, and books. The commission is 100 euros. The question is ONLY: how do you value each touchpoint? Give a baseline, a better version, and how you would check it.
back: Baseline: last-click, all 100 to the last touch; simple and what most reporting uses. Better: a data-driven split, e.g. Markov removal effect or Shapley, from many journeys with and without each channel. Check: an incrementality test, switching one channel off in some regions and comparing bookings. Stop there: what to do with the values (budget, bidding) is the next question, and nobody asked it yet.
